title: Courage
hook: steady in hard things, neither reckless nor cowardly

segments.voice: Yesterday, justice: giving each their due, in money, in honor, in thanks. Your line was each their due. Which debt did you pay? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-nine.

Queen Esther has a problem with a door. Behind it sits the Persian king, and the law says anyone who walks in uncalled is put to death, unless the king holds out his golden scepter. Her people are about to be destroyed, and she is the one inside the palace. Her cousin Mordecai sends her a message that ends with a question: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" Esther could stay quiet and safe. She could storm in. What she actually does is today's virtue, the one the old Latin lists call fortitude.

Fortitude is courage with its feet planted. Christian teachers describe it as a middle path between two failures: the coward who won't face the hard thing, and the reckless one who charges at it without thinking. Watch Esther walk that path. First, she doesn't rush. She sends word to Mordecai to gather her people and fast for her, and she and her maids will fast too. Then she says: "and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish." That's not bravado. She's counted the cost and decided. And when she does walk through the door, she doesn't blurt out the whole crisis. The king holds out the scepter, and she invites him to a banquet. She chooses her moment. Courage and prudence, working together. In the Bible, the call to courage can come with a reason attached. God tells Joshua: "Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest." The courage isn't self-made. It rests on not being alone. And Paul writes to Timothy: "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind." Power and a sound mind, side by side. Steady, not wild. Jews read Esther's story aloud at Purim, and some Christians read it as a picture of a frightened person who walks through the door anyway.

Here's the practice: find one brave small thing. Settle, and breathe. Name something you've been avoiding because it scares you a little: a phone call, a hard conversation, a doctor's appointment, telling someone the truth. Don't solve it yet. Just do what Esther did first: get still, and prepare. Picture yourself doing it calmly. Plant your feet on the floor. If you pray, you can hold Joshua's words: be strong and of a good courage. The bell holds the time.
Fortitude. Steady courage in hard things: neither running from them nor charging in blind. One of the cardinal virtues.

Your line: steady courage. Today, do the brave small thing you named, prepared and calm, and if your knees shake, let them. Esther went in not knowing how it would end. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Christian moral teaching names fortitude among the cardinal virtues and among the gifts of the Spirit in Catholic teaching; some Christians pray for courage before hard tasks, and the story of Esther is read in churches and at the Jewish festival of Purim.

fork.setup: you're Esther. your people are in danger, and going to the king uncalled could cost your life. what do you do?
options: stay quiet; you might be spared.
ask your people to fast with you, then go in, whatever the cost.
storm in at once and denounce the plot.
fork.reveal: she prepares, then goes: "and if I perish, I perish." and once inside, she invites the king to a banquet and picks her moment.

original.note: Latin: strength, steadiness; the name Latin-speaking Christian teachers gave this virtue.

trapdoor: what you thought: courage means feeling no fear.
what it means: steady courage in hard things, neither running nor charging in blind.
what a scholar hears: Esther pairs courage with preparation and timing: a fast first, then a banquet before the request.

notes: Esther 4:11 paraphrased (death for coming uncalled unless the golden scepter is held out); 4:16 the fast (the text's 'three days' omitted); 5:1–4 the scepter and the banquet invitation.
Fortitude as a mean between cowardice and rashness is attributed to 'Christian teachers' (Aquinas, following Aristotle); confirm.
howItsDone: fortitude (fortitudo) as one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit in Catholic teaching (Isaiah 11:2 in the Vulgate tradition); confirm.
